Abstract
Traditional analysis of bloodstain patterns and shoeprints relies on manual visual examination,
which is subjective, time-consuming, and prone to variability between experts. This report stud-
ies a deep-learning framework that automates two forensic tasks: (a) classiﬁcation of bloodstain
patterns and (b) prediction of demographic attributes from footprint impressions. A Vision Trans-
former (ViT-Base/16) trained on approximately 2,700 labeled bloodstain photographs distinguishes
ﬁve pattern classes—drip, impact, cast-oﬀ, transfer, and expirated—and reaches an overall classi-
ﬁcation accuracy of 94.3%. A ResNet-18 network trained on 2,400 barefoot images from the UNB
StepUP-P150 dataset predicts gender, height, and age group through multi-task learning, with a
gender classiﬁcation

aset predicts gender, height, and age group through multi-task learning, with a
gender classiﬁcation accuracy of 91.6%. Both modules share a common preprocessing pipeline and
produce probabilistic conﬁdence scores, scenario hypotheses, and automated reports through a web
application, improving the objectivity, eﬃciency, and standardization of forensic evidence analysis.
The report covers the related literature, datasets, system design, results, strengths, limitations, and
directions for future work.

1. Introduction
Chapter 1
Introduction
Crime Scene Investigation (CSI) is crucial for recreating the circumstances of a crime and generating
authentic evidence for court. Bloodstain patterns and shoe print analysis help provide a wealth
of information about an individual’s actions, gait and some individual traits during and after the
crime. Bloodstain Pattern Analysis (BPA) provides valuable information regarding the cause of
the bloodshed, such as dripping, impact, cast oﬀand transfer. Footprints can help recreate an
individual’s gait, and also gives estimates on their gender, height range and age group.
However both require a large degree of visualisation and investigation by experts. This can result

.
However both require a large degree of visualisation and investigation by experts. This can result
in variation between experts, and introduce bias. Both can be problematic in complex, degraded
or partially contaminated evidence. Footprints can appear incomplete and distorted which makes
the analysis challenging. Comparing footprints to databases can take a long time, and can also
result in a large amount of potential errors. There is a need for automated, objective and scalable
analysis tools.
Machine learning has already been used in the forensic sector to classify blood spatter, match
shoeprints and identify victim demographics. However there are limitations. Most are single evi-
dence types, not using machine learning across a variety of individually relevant evidence. Sample
sizes t

types, not using machine learning across a variety of individually relevant evidence. Sample
sizes tend to be small or controlled environments. Outputs are also deterministic, with no proba-
bility present. There is no consolidated framework using a variety of evidence.
This seminar will investigate a consolidated deep learning framework [1] proposed by Murugan
et al. This uses a (a) multi-class classiﬁcation of bloodstain patterns using a Vision Transformer
(ViT-Base/16), and (b) identiﬁcation of demographics from footprint impressions using ResNet-18
convolutional neural networks. Probabilistic outputs and automated reporting are produced.

Literature Survey

Towards a Likelihood Ratio Approach to Bloodstain Pattern
Analysis (Zou and Stern, 2022)
Zou and Stern employed quantitative elliptical stain variables into a bivariate gaussian likelihood
ratio model for point of origin classiﬁcation between impact and gunshot bloodstains. This provides
a statistical approach for comparing the evidence however lacks any attempt to classify between
more general bloodstain mechanism types.

3. Materials and Methods
Chapter 3
Materials and Methods
3.1
Datasets
Publicly available forensic datasets were used to train and validate the system, which supports
reproducibility and unbiased evaluation.
• Bloodstain dataset: Roughly 2,700 labeled bloodstain photographs retrieved from the
CSAFE, Noblis, Figshare, and Mendeley repositories. The dataset contains ﬁve equally rep-
resented classes: drip, impact, cast-oﬀ, transfer, and expirated. The ground truth labels come
from annotations in the datasets together with expert-generated metadata.
• Footprint dataset: 2,400 barefoot footprint images from the UNB StepUP-P150 dataset.
Each image carries ground-truth labels for the gender, height, and age g

he UNB StepUP-P150 dataset.
Each image carries ground-truth labels for the gender, height, and age group of the person
who left the footprint.
3.2
Preprocessing and Data Preparation
All input images undergo a standard preprocessing pipeline to improve robustness and generaliza-
tion, so that features are extracted consistently irrespective of how the images were obtained. The
steps, applied in sequence, are:
• Noise reduction: Gaussian ﬁlters are applied to reduce noise.
• Background removal: Thresholding and masking of contours remove the background.
• Normalization: Pixel intensities are normalized to lie between 0 and 1.
• Resizing: Images of both datasets are resized to 224 × 224 pixels for compatibility with the
deep learning architectures.
• Splitting: Each dataset is divided in a no

for compatibility with the
deep learning architectures.
• Splitting: Each dataset is divided in a non-overlapping manner into 70% for training, 15%
for validation, and 15% for testing.

3.4
Experimental Setup
The experiments were carried out on a PC with an Intel® Core i7 processor running at 3.2 GHz

4. Methodology
Chapter 4
Methodology
4.1
Design Rationale and System Overview
This framework provides an AI-enabled decision support tool to help understand bloodstain pat-
terns and footprints using deep learning techniques to provide quality evidence for criminal inves-
tigations. It has the capability to analyse images from a variety of sources such as digital camera
photos or footprint images acquired in a controlled setting. As all of the evidence images pass
through the same preprocessing steps, the features extracted will be consistent between the evi-
dence types. There are two analysis modules which work together to ﬁrstly identify the mechanism
and type of bloodstain produced using the bloods

hich work together to ﬁrstly identify the mechanism
and type of bloodstain produced using the bloodstain pattern analysis module, and secondly to
extract demographic and anthropometric properties of the footprint using the footprint analysis
module.
4.2
System Workﬂow
The workﬂow in Figure 4.1 has four major steps:
1. Image ingestion and pre-processing: Evidence images are captured and processed through
the standardised pipeline (Gaussian ﬁlter, background removal, normalisation).
2. Blood pattern recognition: Blood evidence is processed through the pipeline. First blood
is identiﬁed (blood or not blood with conﬁdence score and thresholding). If blood is present,
then the pattern is identiﬁed using the Vision Transformer. If no blood is identiﬁed, then the
image is labelled and this step s

d using the Vision Transformer. If no blood is identiﬁed, then the
image is labelled and this step skipped.
3. Footprint demographic prediction: Footprints are processed through the pipeline. Fea-
tures such as length, width and heel width are extracted, quality checked and normalised. A
CNN with regression is used to predict gender, height and age.
4. Interpretation and report creation: The two pipelines are fed into a reporting dashboard.
This provides a summary of the evidence including predictions, graphs and conﬁdence scores.

4. Methodology
Figure 4.1: Proposed system workﬂow.
This can be exported as a report.
4.3
Bloodstain Pattern Analysis Module
This module classiﬁes the images based on the mechanism of formation. A Vision Transformer
(ViT-Base/16) is used here. Unlike the traditional convolutional network that uses local receptive
ﬁelds, the Vision Transformer can capture global long range spatial dependencies making it very
useful for analysing complex bloodstain patterns.
Input images are resized to 224×224 pixels, split into patches of ﬁxed size (for the standard ViT-
Base/16 conﬁguration, 16×16 pixels), and embedded into the transformer. The transformer encoder
layers process the patch embeddings, and the output is

nto the transformer. The transformer encoder
layers process the patch embeddings, and the output is a probability score over ﬁve bloodstain
classes: drip, impact, cast-oﬀ, transfer, and expirated.
4.4
Footprint Analysis Module
The footprint module analyses footprint images to produce demographic morphology proﬁles from
both barefoot and shoe prints. A ResNet-18 CNN was used for feature extraction and classiﬁcation.
This was due to its fast processing time, reliability and known success in identiﬁcation based on
images. The algorithm can learn unique features such as foot size, toe deﬁnition and heel pressure
to classify what type of morphology a foot has.

4. Methodology
This module uses a multi-task network to predict gender and age group (classiﬁcation). As well
as predicting height (regression). The network uses categorical cross entropy loss to predict gender
and age group. Mean square error loss is used to approximate the height of the person.
4.5
Interpretation and Reporting
Rather than providing deterministic results, this provides probabilistic conﬁdence values. When
analysing a bloodstain image the programme gives the user information on how conﬁdent it is that
the stain is blood or non-blood. It also gives information on what mechanism is most likely and
the top scenarios with supporting factors. This includes things such as how much of the sta

kely and
the top scenarios with supporting factors. This includes things such as how much of the stain is
made up of ﬁne droplets, how round the stain is and how streaky the stain is. When analysing a
footprint image, the programme will give information on the estimated shoe size, estimated height,
age group, sex prediction and the scale used. This increases objectivity when evaluating hypotheses.

5.2
Qualitative Bloodstain Interpretation
Figures 5.1 and 5.2 show outputs of the system for several bloodstain images. The model correlated
speciﬁc visual traits with their formation mechanisms:
• Distributions of ﬁne droplets were accurately associated with impact mechanisms.
• Evenly spaced, vertically oriented stains were identiﬁed as drip patterns.
• A misty appearance with a high density of droplets was classiﬁed as gunshot backspatter.

Figure 5.1: System outputs for a radial impact burst, a transfer smear, gunshot back spatter, and

• Stains distributed outwardly in a circular pattern around a point of origin were identiﬁed as

with supporting cues. The hypothesis scores are modest and sometimes clo

9. Conclusion
Chapter 9
Conclusion
The framework studied in this seminar is an accurate dual-task deep learning system for analyzing
bloodstain patterns and footprint demographics. A Vision Transformer classiﬁes ﬁve bloodstain
patterns with an overall accuracy of 94.3%, and a ResNet-18 network predicts gender from footprints
with an accuracy of 91.6%. Because both modules share one preprocessing pipeline and report
through a single web application, the system oﬀers an objective and fast alternative to manual
visual inspection.
By outputting probabilistic conﬁdence scores instead of deterministic labels, the approach sup-
ports forensic reasoning and hypothesis evaluation.

Appendix D
Viva Questions and Answers
Common Viva Questions
1. What was the main concept behind the framework?
Answer: A single uniﬁed framework providing AI-assisted support in decision-making. This
framework includes deep learning algorithms trained to automatically analyse evidence. The
ﬁrst being a Vision Transformer to classify bloodstain evidence. Secondly, the algorithm uses
a ResNet-18 network to predict gender, height, and age group from footprint evidence. Each
model outputs probability conﬁdence levels.
2. Why is the Vision Transformer used on bloodstain samples?
Answer: The Vision Transformer provides global long-distance relationships within an image.
This is o

nswer: The Vision Transformer provides global long-distance relationships within an image.
This is opposed to using convolutional networks which have local receptive ﬁelds. This makes
it more eﬀective for complex bloodstain patterns.
3. Why was ResNet-18 used on footprint samples?
Answer: ResNet-18 was selected due to its eﬃciency. It has been proved to be eﬃcient at
image-based biometric identiﬁcation. It is also very light.
4. What preprocessing and data preparation steps are used?
Answer: Gaussian ﬁltering to reduce noise, thresholding and contour masking to remove the
background, normalization of pixel values to the range 0–1, and resizing to 224×224. The data
are split 70:15:15 into training, validation, and test sets, and the training data are augmented
by rotation, ﬂipping, scaling,

ining, validation, and test sets, and the training data are augmented
by rotation, ﬂipping, scaling, and brightness changes.
5. How does the multi-task footprint network learn?
Answer: It performs gender and age group classiﬁcation with categorical cross-entropy loss
and height estimation as a regression task with mean squared error loss, learning all three

6. Why are probabilistic outputs important?
Answer: They let forensic practitioners weigh alternative scenario hypotheses instead of ac-

ability near 0.5 also warns that a prediction is uncertain.
7. What results were reported?

91.6% accuracy (F1: 91.0%) for gender classiﬁcation.
